issues: there was once a Buddha tooth here, which was tall, broad, and magnificent → 昔有佛齒，高廣嚴麗: the stūpa formerly held a Buddha tooth and was tall, broad and magnificent (Mizutani: 仏の歯が収納されていて高くもあり広くもありりっぱな)
en_revised: Two li to the east of the city is a stūpa over three hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is constructed of piled stone rising prominently, with exquisite carvings and a unique design; it is the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya (釋迦菩薩) encountered the Buddha Dīpankara (然燈佛), spread out his deerskin garment, and laid down his hair to cover the mud, thereby receiving his prediction. Although aeons have passed and the world has been destroyed, this trace has not vanished. On certain fast days, the heavens rain down various flowers, and the populace, vying in their devotion, perform offerings. To its west is a saṃghārāma with few monks. Further to the south is a small stūpa; this is the site where the mud was once covered, which King Aśoka built in this secluded spot to avoid the main road. Inside the city are the old foundations of a great stūpa. I have heard from the records of the ancients that it formerly held a Buddha tooth and was tall, broad, and magnificent. Now that the tooth is gone, only the old foundations remain. Beside it is a stūpa over thirty feet high. Local tradition says, without knowing its origin, that it descended from the sky and established its base here. Since it was not made by human hands, it possesses many spiritual marvels. More than ten li to the southwest of the city is a stūpa marking the spot where the Tathāgata, traveling through the air from Central India to convert beings, descended; the people of the country, moved by admiration, built this spiritual foundation. Not far to its east is a stūpa where the Bodhisattva Śākya once encountered the Buddha Dīpankara and purchased flowers.

issues: a *stūpa* of prediction → 受記窣堵波: the Prediction Stūpa just described (Mizutani: 受記翠堵波) | because of its compassionate nature → 以慈善故: because of [my] compassion and goodness (Mizutani: 我が慈善の心により) | spoke of the aggregates and realms → 說蘊界處: aggregates, elements and sense-bases
en_revised: Traveling over twenty *li* southwest of the city to a small rocky ridge, there is a monastery with lofty halls and multi-storied pavilions, constructed from piled stones. The courtyards and buildings are desolate, and there are absolutely no monks. In the center is a *stūpa* over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Southwest of the monastery is a deep, precipitous ravine with a waterfall flowing down and cliffs standing like walls. On the stone wall of the eastern cliff is a large cave, which is the dwelling place of the dragon Gopāla (瞿波羅龍). The entrance path is narrow, the cave is dark and gloomy, the cliff rocks drip with moisture, and the path is wet with the remaining flow. In the past, there was a shadow of the Buddha, shining as if it were his true form, with all the marks and characteristics complete, appearing just as if he were present. Since recent times, people have not been able to see it fully; even if they do see it, it is only indistinctly. Those who pray with utmost sincerity and have a spiritual response may see it clearly for a moment, but it cannot last long. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, this dragon was a cowherd who supplied milk and curds to the king, but he failed to present them properly. Having been reprimanded, he harbored resentment in his heart; he then used gold coins to buy flowers to offer to the Stūpa of the Prediction (受記窣堵波), wishing to become a wicked dragon to destroy the country and harm the king. He then rushed to the stone wall and threw himself to his death. Consequently, he resided in this cave and became a great dragon king, intending to emerge from the cave to fulfill his evil vow. Just as this thought arose, the Tathāgata perceived it. Compassionate toward the people of this country who were about to be harmed by the dragon, he exercised his supernatural powers and arrived from Central India. When the dragon saw the Tathāgata, his poisonous intent ceased; he accepted the precept against killing and vowed to protect the True Dharma. The dragon then requested the Tathāgata, "May you always reside in this cave, and may your holy disciples constantly receive my offerings." The Tathāgata replied, "I am about to enter nirvana, but I shall leave my shadow for you and send five arhats to constantly receive your offerings. Even when the True Dharma has faded away, this practice shall not cease. If your poisonous heart should flare up in anger, you should look upon the shadow I have left behind; because of my compassion and goodness, your poisonous heart will cease. In this Bhadrakalpa, the World-Honored Ones who are yet to come will also have compassion for you and will all leave their images behind." Outside the entrance of the Shadow Cave (佛影窟), there are two square stones. On one of the stones is the footprint of the Tathāgata, where the wheel mark is faintly visible and light occasionally shines forth. To the left and right of the Shadow Cave are many stone chambers, all of which are places where the various holy disciples of the Tathāgata entered into meditative concentration. In the northwest corner of the Shadow Cave is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata used to walk. Beside it is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Not far from this is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata manifested and expounded the True Doctrine, and where he spoke of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (蘊界處). To the west of the Shadow Cave is a large flat rock where the Tathāgata once washed his kaṣāya robe, and the faint traces of its pattern are still visible.

issues: *nā* (crabapple) → 㮈 nai, crab-apple | fine *nü* (a type of fine cotton or wool fabric) → 細㲲: fine cotton cloth | see the Tathāgata’s skull bone (fee clause) → 頂骨: crown bone, as earlier in the passage (skull = 髑髏骨)
en_revised: Thirty-some *li* southeast of the city, one arrives at the city of Haḍḍa (醯羅城). It is four or five *li* in circumference, with steep and rugged defenses, and flower groves and ponds that are bright, fresh, and clear as mirrors. The people living in the city are honest, simple, and possess upright faith. There is a multi-storied pavilion with painted beams and vermilion pillars. In the second story of the pavilion is a small stupa made of the seven precious substances, in which the crown bone of the Tathāgata is placed. The bone is one foot and two inches in circumference, with distinct hair pores, and its color is yellowish-white; it is contained in a precious casket and placed inside the stupa. Those who wish to know the signs of their good or evil karma mix incense powder with clay and press it onto the crown bone; according to the response of their merit, the patterns appear clearly. There is another small stupa made of the seven precious substances to store the Tathāgata’s skull bone, which is shaped like a lotus leaf and is the same color as the crown bone; it is also kept sealed within a precious casket. There is another small stupa made of the seven precious substances containing the Tathāgata’s eyeball, which is as large as a *nai* (㮈, crab-apple) fruit, brilliant and transparent, shining through from inside to out; it is also kept sealed within a precious casket. The Tathāgata’s *saṃghāṭī* (monastic robe) is made of fine cotton cloth (㲲), its color is yellowish-red, and it is kept in a precious casket; as the years have been long, it is slightly damaged. The Tathāgata’s *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) has rings made of white iron and a shaft made of sandalwood; it is kept in a precious tube. Recently, a king heard that all these objects were things the Tathāgata had personally used in the past, and relying on his power, he forcibly took them away. Once they arrived in his own country, he placed them in the palace where he resided, but before even twelve days had passed, when he sought them, they were already lost; upon further searching, they had already returned to their original place. These five sacred sites possess many spiritual wonders, and the king of Kapiśa (迦畢試國) has appointed five pure-practitioners (brahmacārins) to provide incense and flowers in service to them. Pilgrims coming to pay their respects arrive in an unbroken succession. The pure-practitioners, desiring to pursue emptiness and tranquility, and considering that wealth is something people value, have provisionally established a schedule of fees to put an end to the clamor and confusion. The general outline is as follows: those who wish to see the Tathāgata’s crown bone must pay a tax of one gold coin; if they wish to take an impression, they must pay a tax of five gold coins; for the remaining items, there is a graded schedule of fees. Although the fees are heavy, the number of those coming to pay their respects only increases. To the northwest of the multi-storied pavilion is a stūpa, which is also very tall and displays many spiritual wonders; if a person touches it with a finger, it immediately begins to shake, its very foundations tilt and move, and its bells ring in harmony.

issues: Persia (Pārśva) → 波剌斯 = Persia (Pārasa); Pārśva is the name of 脇尊者
en_revised: Inside the royal city, to the northeast, there is an old foundation; it was formerly the precious pedestal of the Buddha’s alms bowl. After the Tathāgata entered nirvana, the bowl drifted to this country, where it was formally worshipped for several hundred years; it then circulated through various countries and is now in Persia (波剌斯, Pārasa). Eight or nine li to the southeast of the city, there is a Pippala tree (卑鉢羅樹) over a hundred feet high, with wide-spreading branches and leaves that provide a dense shade. The four Buddhas of the past have already sat beneath it, and images of these four Buddhas still exist there today. During the Bhadrakalpa, the nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas will all sit there as well. Deities guard and protect it, and its spiritual influence is secretly bestowed. The Śākya Tathāgata once sat under this tree facing south and told Ānanda: "Four hundred years after I pass away, a king will appear in the world named Kaniṣka; not far to the south of this spot, he will erect a stūpa, and a great portion of the relics of my bones and flesh will be gathered within it."

issues: I have heard from the elders that in the beginning → 聞諸先志曰: from the records of the ancients (the earlier 聞諸耆舊 is 'elders')
en_revised: To the south of the Pippala tree is a stupa built by King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王). Four hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, King Kaniṣka ascended the throne and ruled over Jambudvīpa. He did not believe in merit or demerit and slighted the Buddha’s Dharma. While hunting in the marshes, he encountered a white rabbit; the king personally gave chase, but it suddenly vanished at this spot. He saw a young cowherd among the trees making a small stupa three feet in height. The king asked, "What are you doing?" The cowherd replied, "Long ago, the holy wisdom of Śākya Buddha prophesied: 'A king will appear who shall build a stupa on this excellent site, and many of my bodily relics will be gathered within it.' Your Majesty’s holy virtues were cultivated in the past, your name matches the ancient prophecy, and your divine merit and superior fortune are destined for this very moment; therefore, I have come ahead to alert and inspire you." Having said this, he suddenly disappeared. Hearing these words, the king was filled with joy and reverence. Reflecting on his name and the Great Sage’s prior prophecy, he developed true faith and deeply respected the Buddha’s Dharma. Around the small stupa, he built a stone stupa, wishing to use his power to cover it completely. Yet, as he increased the height, the small stupa always emerged three feet above it. Only when the height exceeded four hundred feet—with the base standing one and a half li in circumference and a five-tiered foundation one hundred and fifty feet high—was he finally able to cover the small stupa. The king, rejoicing at this auspicious event, further erected twenty-five tiers of gilded copper rings above it, and placing one hu of the Tathāgata’s relics within them, he performed offerings in this manner. No sooner was the construction finished than he saw the small stupa protruding halfway out from beneath the southeast corner of the great foundation. The king was displeased and cast it away; it then lodged halfway within the stone base under the second tier of the stupa, while another small stupa emerged once more at its original location. The king then withdrew and sighed, saying: "Alas, human efforts are easily misguided, but divine merit is difficult to conceal. When supported by the holy and spiritual, what can anger achieve?" Having felt shame and fear, he confessed his fault and returned. Those two stupas are still present today; those who are afflicted with illness and wish to pray for recovery apply incense and scatter flowers, and with sincere devotion take refuge, most of them obtaining a cure. To the south of the stone steps on the eastern face of the great stupa, two stupas are carved, one three feet high and the other five feet high, their design and shape modeled after the great stupa. Two Buddha images are also fashioned, one four feet high and the other six feet high, imitating the seated image with crossed legs under the Mahā-bodhi tree; when the sunlight shines upon them, the golden color glitters brilliantly, and as the shadows gradually shift, the stone patterns appear dark blue. I have heard from the elders that several hundred years ago, there were golden ants in the crevices of the stone base, the large ones like fingers and the small ones like grains of wheat, which followed one another to gnaw at the stone wall, the patterns appearing as if carved and inlaid with gold sand, forming these images, which are still present today. On the southern side of the stone steps of the great stūpa (大窣堵波) there is a painted Buddha image sixteen feet high; from the chest upward it appears as two bodies, but from the chest downward it is joined into one. I have heard from the records of the ancients that in the beginning, there was a poor man who supported himself by manual labor and, having obtained one gold coin, wished to have a Buddha image made. He went to the place of the stūpa and said to a painter, "I now wish to depict the exquisite features of the Tathāgata (如來), but I have only one gold coin, which is insufficient to reward your labor; I have long cherished this desire but am burdened by worry, being constrained by my poverty." At that time, the painter, perceiving his utmost sincerity, did not speak of the price but promised to complete the work. Later, there was another man whose circumstances were the same as the former; he brought a gold coin and requested that an image of the Buddha be painted. The painter then accepted the money from both men, sought out excellent pigments, and painted a single image for them both. When the two men came on the same day to pay their respects, the painter pointed to the one image, showed it to them, and said, "This is the Buddha image you commissioned." The two men looked at each other, as if they had some misgivings. The painter, knowing their doubts in his heart, said to the two men, "Why are you so long in thought? Whatever I have received, I have not diminished by even a hair's breadth. If these words are not false, the image will surely manifest a divine transformation." Before his voice had ceased, the image manifested a miracle: the bodies separated and their shadows intertwined, and the light of the image shone brilliantly. The two men were convinced and filled with faith and joy. More than a hundred paces to the southwest of the great stupa (mahāstūpa), there is a white stone Buddha image eighteen feet high, standing and facing north; it possesses many divine signs and frequently emits light. At times, people have seen the image go out at night to walk, circumambulating the great stupa. Recently, a group of thieves intended to enter and commit theft, but the image went out to meet them; the band of thieves was terrified and retreated, and the image returned to its original place, standing as before. Because of this, the group of thieves reformed and renewed themselves, traveling through the towns and villages to tell everyone, far and near. To the left and right of the great stupa, there are hundreds of small stupas arranged like fish scales. The Buddha images are adorned with the utmost craftsmanship, and extraordinary fragrances and strange sounds are sometimes heard; divine immortals and sages are occasionally seen circumambulating them. Regarding this stupa, the Tathāgata prophesied that it would be burned seven times and rebuilt seven times, at which point the Buddhadharma would come to an end. The records of the ancients state that it has already been built and destroyed three times. When I first arrived in this country, I happened to encounter a great fire, and I saw it being constructed, though it was not yet completed.

issues: the King immediately bestowed one hundred million gold coins upon him → 如意論師一使人剃髮，輒賜一億金錢: Manoratha himself, having once had a man shave his head, at once gave him 100 million coins; hence the king's shame at being outdone (Mizutani: 如意論師は、一度、人に髪を剃らせて、たちどころに一億の金銭を与えた) | lost his way … offered a reward … to anyone who could find and track it → 逐豕失蹤，有尋知迹者，賞一億金錢: lost the boar's track; someone found the trail and was rewarded 100 million (Mizutani: 見つけ出したものがあったので…とらせた) | summoned the various non-Buddhists to debate with Manoratha → 召諸外道與如意論者: summoned the non-Buddhists who had debated with Manoratha (now dead) (Mizutani: 如意と論議をした外道の人たちを召集し)
en_revised: To the west of the great stūpa is an old monastery (saṃghārāma), which was built by King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王). It has multi-storied pavilions and tiered halls, with layered terraces and open windows; it was built to summon high-ranking monks and to manifest auspicious blessings. Although it is now dilapidated, it is still considered a marvelous work of craftsmanship. The number of monks has decreased, and they all study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Since the monastery was built, extraordinary people have appeared there one after another. The masters who composed treatises and those who attained the holy fruits have left behind a pure influence that still circulates, and their supreme virtues have not been extinguished. On the third story of the pavilion is the room of the Venerable Pārśva (波栗濕縛尊者), which has long since collapsed, though a commemorative marker still stands. Originally, when the Venerable was a teacher of the Brahmins (梵志), he was nearly eighty years old when he left his home and donned the dyed robes. The youths in the city mocked him, saying: "What a foolish, decrepit old man, how shallow his wisdom! Those who leave home have two duties: first, to practice meditation; second, to recite the scriptures. Now, in your senility, you have made no progress; you merely clutter the ranks of the pure and know only how to eat your fill." When the Venerable Pārśva heard these reproaches, he took leave of the people of the time and made a vow, saying: "If I do not master the principles of the Tripiṭaka, sever the desires of the three realms, attain the six supernatural powers, and possess the eight liberations, I shall never let my ribs (脇) touch a mat!" From then on, he felt only that the days were insufficient; whether walking, sitting, or standing in contemplation, he studied the doctrines by day and practiced quiet meditation with a concentrated mind by night. After three years had passed, he had mastered the Tripiṭaka, severed the desires of the three realms, and attained the three types of clear wisdom (trividyā). The people of the time respected him and thus called him the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者). To the east of the room of the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) is an old chamber where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論); people respect it and have sealed it to mark the site. More than fifty paces to the south of Vasubandhu’s room is a second-story pavilion where the master Manoratha (末笯曷剌他) composed the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘婆沙論). This master appeared in the world one thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. In his youth, he was fond of learning and possessed talent and eloquence; his reputation reached far and wide, and both the clergy and the laity turned their hearts toward him. At that time, King Vikramāditya (毘訖羅摩阿迭多) of the country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) extended his majestic influence to distant lands and brought all of India under his rule; every day he distributed five hundred million gold coins to provide for the poor, the destitute, the orphaned, and the solitary. The treasurer, fearing that the national resources would be exhausted, offered a remonstrance, saying: "Your Majesty’s awe-inspiring power reaches foreign peoples and your benevolence extends even to insects; I pray you increase the distribution by another five hundred million gold coins to relieve the needy of the four quarters. Once the treasury is empty, we shall have to levy further taxes on the landholders; when heavy taxation continues without end and the cries of resentment spread everywhere, then the sovereign above will enjoy the reputation of being a generous provider, while the ministers below will bear the blame for being disrespectful." The King replied: "I gather the surplus to provide for the insufficient; I do not do this for the sake of personal luxury or the squandering of national resources." He then added another five hundred million to bestow upon the poor and needy. Later, while hunting, he chased a boar and lost its track; someone found the trail, and he rewarded him with one hundred million gold coins. The master Manoratha, for his part, once had a man shave his head and at once gave him one hundred million gold coins, which the state historians recorded accordingly. The King felt ashamed to be outdone and was constantly vexed in his heart, wishing to publicly humiliate the master Manoratha. He then summoned one hundred practitioners of heterodox schools who were of high virtue and profound learning, and issued an order, saying: "Desiring to focus my attention and wander in the true realms, yet finding the heterodox paths to be chaotic and my mind at a loss as to where to turn, I shall now examine their relative merits so that I may focus my devotion on the most excellent." When the time came for the debate, he issued a further order, saying: "The heterodox masters are all men of talent; the assembly of Śramaṇas should be well-versed in their own doctrines. If they win, I shall honor the Buddha-Dharma; if they lose, I shall execute the monks." Thereupon, Manoratha (如意) questioned the various heterodox teachers, and ninety-nine of them had already retreated in defeat. Regarding the one person remaining in the lower seat, he looked upon him with contempt and engaged in a heated debate, which turned to the subject of fire and smoke. The king and the heterodox teacher both shouted out: "Master Manoratha’s words and reasoning are flawed! For smoke to precede fire is the constant principle of things." Although Manoratha wished to explain the difficulty, no one would listen. Ashamed at being publicly humiliated, he bit off his tongue and wrote a warning to his disciple Vasubandhu (世親), saying: "Among a crowd of partisans, do not contend for the great truth; among the confused masses, do not argue for the correct doctrine." Having finished speaking, he died. Not long after, the king Vikramāditya (超日王) lost his kingdom, and a new king rose to power who valued the wise and virtuous. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to wash away the previous shame, came and addressed the king, saying: "Great King, you rule with holy virtue and are the master and life-force of all sentient beings. My late teacher Manoratha had mastered the most profound mysteries, yet the former king, harboring an old grudge, humiliated his great reputation before the masses; having received his guidance and instruction, I wish to avenge the grievance done to my predecessor." The king, knowing that Manoratha (如意) was a man of wisdom and admiring the noble character of Vasubandhu (世親), summoned the non-Buddhists (外道) who had debated with Manoratha. Vasubandhu restated the principles of his predecessor, and the non-Buddhists, admitting defeat, withdrew.

issues: gave his father the king’s great elephant → 以父王大象施: gave his father the king's great elephant (wording ambiguous in DM) | the logician Īśvara → 伊濕伐邏論師: the śāstra-master Īśvara
en_revised: To the north of the city is a stūpa, which is where Prince Sudāna (蘇達拏) gave the great elephant of his father the king to a Brahmin, and having been rebuked and banished, looked back to thank the people of the country and bid them farewell after passing through the city gate. Beside it is a saṃghārāma with more than fifty monks, all of whom are students of the Hīnayāna. In the past, the śāstra-master Īśvara (伊濕伐邏) composed the *Abhidharma-pradīpa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨明燈論) here.

issues: the great mountain (Pravaragiri) → 至大山: a great mountain; the name Pravaragiri is not in the text
en_revised: Traveling over a hundred *li* to the northwest from the rishi’s hut and crossing a small mountain, one reaches a great mountain. On the southern side of the mountain is a monastery with few monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna. Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the place where the One-Horned Rishi (Ekashṛṅga-ṛṣi) formerly resided. The rishi was seduced and led astray by a courtesan, causing him to lose his supernatural powers, and the courtesan then rode upon his shoulders to return to the city.

issues: Mount Cong (崇山) → 至崇山: a lofty mountain, not a name (Mizutani: 高い山に至る)
en_revised: Fifty-some *li* to the northeast of the city of Varusa (跋虜沙城), one arrives at a lofty mountain (崇山). On the mountain, there is a blue stone image of the wife of Maheśvara (大自在天), who is the goddess Bhīmā (毘摩天女). According to local tradition, this celestial image appeared there naturally. Because it is highly miraculous, there are many who come to pray; people from all the countries of India, whether noble or humble, gather here from far and near to seek blessings and make vows. For those who wish to see the form of the celestial deity, if they are sincere and single-minded and fast for seven days, some may obtain a vision, and most of their prayers are fulfilled. At the foot of the mountain, there is a temple of Maheśvara where ash-smearing heretics (塗灰外道) perform their ritual worship.

issues: converted the later followers → 化波爾尼仙後進: converted a later follower of Pāṇini (the boy of the story) | Five hundred years after → 垂五百年: nearly five hundred years | stray closing quotation mark after the bats sentence (the Arhat's speech continues to 'beyond words')
en_revised: Traveling over twenty li northwest from the city of Udakhāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), one reaches the town of Śalātura (婆羅覩邏邑), which is the birthplace of the ṛṣi Pāṇini (波爾尼仙), the author of the Śabdavidyā-śāstra (聲明論). At the beginning of remote antiquity, written characters were numerous and extensive, but as time passed through the kalpa of destruction, the world became a void, until the long-lived deities descended to inspire both the sacred and the secular, and from this, literary records were born. Since that time, their sources have proliferated. King Brahmā and Lord Indra created models according to the needs of the times, and the various immortals of heterodox paths each devised their own scripts; people followed their predecessors and vied to practice what was handed down, but students' efforts were in vain, as it was difficult to investigate the systems in detail. When the human lifespan was one hundred years, there was the ṛṣi Pāṇini, who was born with great wisdom and broad learning. Pitying the decadence of the age, he wished to prune away the superficial and false, and to edit and refine the cumbersome and redundant. He traveled to various regions to inquire after the Way, and upon meeting Maheśvara (自在天), he expressed his intention to compose a work. Maheśvara said, "Excellent! I shall assist you." Having received these instructions, the ṛṣi withdrew and applied his mind to deep reflection, collecting a vast array of words to compose a lexicon consisting of one thousand stanzas, each containing thirty-two syllables. It exhausted the depths of both the present and the past, and summarized the entirety of literary language. He sealed it and presented it to the king, who found it most extraordinary and issued a decree throughout the kingdom to make it universally studied, rewarding anyone who could recite it with mastery with one thousand gold coins. This is why the tradition of teacher and student has been passed down and flourished in the present age. Consequently, the Brahmins in this town are men of great learning and high talent, possessing broad knowledge and excellent memories. In the town of Śalātura (婆羅覩邏邑) there is a stūpa, which is the place where an Arhat converted a later follower of the sage Pāṇini. Nearly five hundred years after the Tathāgata had passed away, a great Arhat traveling from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) arrived here and saw a Brahmin beating and scolding a young boy. The Arhat asked the Brahmin, "Why are you tormenting this child?" The Brahmin replied, "I am making him study the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (聲明論), but his progress is not timely." The Arhat smiled gently. The old Brahmin said, "The nature of a Śramaṇa is compassion and pity for all living beings. I wish to hear the reason for your laughter." The Arhat said, "It is not easy to speak of this, for I fear it will cause deep doubt. Have you ever heard that the sage Pāṇini composed the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* and left it as a teaching for the world?" The Brahmin replied, "The children of this town, as later followers, look up to his virtue, and his image is still here." The Arhat said, "This child of yours is that very sage. Because he possessed a powerful memory, he indulged in the study of worldly texts, discussing only heterodox doctrines without investigating the true principles. His spiritual wisdom was wasted in vain, and his transmigration has not yet ceased; it is only by riding on the merit of his remaining good deeds that he has become your beloved son. However, the literary expressions of worldly texts merely exhaust one's efforts; how can they compare to the holy teachings of the Tathāgata, which nourish merit and wisdom in the dark? Formerly, on the shore of the Southern Sea, there was a withered tree where five hundred bats lived in holes. Some merchants stopped under this tree. At that time, it was windy and cold, and everyone was hungry and freezing. They gathered firewood and brush, and kindled a fire beneath it. The smoke and flames gradually intensified, and the withered tree caught fire. Among the merchants, there was one trader who, after the middle of the night, recited the Abhidharma-piṭaka. Although those bats were distressed by the fire, they loved the sound of the Dharma so much that they endured it and did not leave, and thus they met their end there. Following their karma, they were reborn, all obtaining human bodies. They left home to study and practice, and by virtue of having heard the sound of the Dharma, they possessed keen intelligence and wisdom, and all attained the holy fruit, becoming fields of merit for the world. Recently, King Kaniṣka and the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) summoned five hundred sages in the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) to compile the Vibhāṣā-śāstra (毘婆沙論); these are the very same five hundred bats from the withered tree. Although I am unworthy, I am one of that number. This shows how the superior and the inferior are truly different, and how the flying and the crawling are vastly distinct. You should now allow your beloved son to leave home; the merit of leaving home is beyond words." When the Arhat had finished speaking these words, he displayed his supernatural powers and suddenly disappeared. The brahmin was deeply moved by awe and wonder, and after exclaiming his admiration for a long time, he told his neighbors everything. He then allowed his son to leave home to study and practice, and subsequently turned to the faith, honoring the Triple Gem. His fellow villagers followed his example, and their devotion remains strong to this day. From the city of Udakahāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), traveling north, crossing mountains and fording rivers for more than six hundred li, one arrives at the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國).

issues: do not achieve success → 好學而不功 'fond of learning but do not apply themselves' (Mizutani: 余りつとめず; Beal: yet have no application)
en_revised: The country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) is over five thousand li in circuit. Mountains and valleys are contiguous, and rivers and marshes connect with the plains. Although grain is sown, the land is not very fertile. There are many grapes but little sugarcane; the land produces gold and iron and is suitable for saffron; the forests are lush, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The cold and heat are temperate, and the winds and rains follow their proper seasons. The people are timid and cowardly, and their customs are deceitful. They are fond of learning but do not apply themselves, and they make incantations their professional skill. They mostly wear white cotton cloth and have few other types of clothing. Although their language differs, it is largely the same as that of India. Their writing and etiquette are quite similar. They highly esteem the Buddhadharma and revere and believe in the Mahāyāna. Along the banks of the Śubhavastu River (蘇婆伐窣堵河), there were formerly one thousand four hundred monasteries, most of which are now desolate. Formerly there were eighteen thousand monks, but now they have gradually decreased. They all study the Mahāyāna and make silent meditation their occupation; they are skilled at reciting the texts but have not yet fathomed their profound meanings. Their moral conduct is pure, and they are especially skilled in incantations. Regarding the traditions of the Vinaya rules, there are five schools: first, the Dharmaguptaka; second, the Mahīśāsaka; third, the Kāśyapīya; fourth, the Sarvāstivāda; and fifth, the Mahāsāṃghika. There are more than ten deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. There are four or five fortified cities, and their king usually governs from the city of Mangala (瞢揭釐城). The city is sixteen or seventeen li in circuit and is densely populated.

issues: at dusk, the flying spray resembles snow → 昏夕飛雪 'in the evening snow flies' (no spray; Mizutani: 朝夕雪を飛ばし; Beal: night snow-drifts are flying)
en_revised: Traveling two hundred and fifty or sixty *li* northeast from the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one enters a great mountain and reaches the Apalāla (阿波邏羅) Dragon Spring, which is the source of the Śubhavastu (蘇婆伐窣堵) River. The stream flows to the southwest; it contains ice during the spring and summer, and in the evening snow flies, the snowflakes shimmering in five colors and radiating light in all directions. As for this dragon, in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was born in the human realm with the name Gangi (殑祇); he was deeply skilled in sorcery and restrained evil dragons from causing torrential rains, so the people of the country relied on him to store surplus grain. The inhabitants and the masses, feeling gratitude and cherishing his virtue, taxed each household one *dou* of grain to present to him. After many years had passed, there were some who defaulted on their payments. Gangi became angry and vowed to become a poisonous dragon, violently unleashing wind and rain to damage the crops. After his life ended, he became the dragon of this pool. The spring flows with white water, damaging the land's productivity. The Śākya Tathāgata, governing the world with great compassion, took pity on the people of this country for suffering this unique disaster and descended to this place, desiring to convert the violent dragon. He had the Vajrapāṇi (執金剛神) strike the mountain cliff with his vajra; the Dragon King was terrified and emerged to take refuge. Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, his mind became pure and he attained faith and enlightenment. The Tathāgata then commanded him not to damage the crops. The dragon said, "Everything I eat depends on the harvest from the people's fields. Now, having received the holy teaching, I fear it will be difficult to sustain myself; I request to collect grain stores once every twelve years." The Tathāgata, in his encompassing compassion, took pity and granted this. Thus, even now, the country suffers the calamity of white water once every twelve years.

Northwest of the country of Kapota (代鴿) → 代鴿西北 'northwest of [the place where he] ransomed the dove' (the Śibi stūpa just described), not a country (Mizutani: 代鴿[本生譚の地]より; Beal: from the place where he redeemed the dove) | deaths followed one after another → read 醫療無功，道死相屬 'the dead lay one after another on the roads' (CBETA punctuates 無功道，死相屬; Mizutani: 道に死者がひき続いた; Beal: the roads were filled with dead)
en_revised: More than two hundred *li* northwest of the place where he ransomed the dove (代鴿), one enters the Sanirāja (珊尼羅闍) River valley and arrives at the Sarpa-auṣadhi (薩裒殺地) monastery. There is a stūpa here, more than eighty feet high. It was here that the Tathāgata, in a former life as Indra (帝釋), encountered a time of famine and widespread pestilence; medical treatments were of no avail, and the dead lay one after another along the roads. Indra, moved by compassion and thinking of how to save them, transformed his body into that of a giant python, lying dead in the valley, and proclaimed to all from the air. Those who heard were moved and rejoiced, rushing to the spot; as they cut pieces from the body, it would grow back, curing their hunger and their illnesses. Not far to the side is a great Soma (蘇摩) stūpa. It was here that the Tathāgata, in a former life as Indra, during a time of pestilence, took pity on all sentient beings and transformed his body into a Soma snake; all who ate of it were restored to health and comfort. Beside the stone cliff to the north of the Sanirāja River, there is a stūpa. Sick people who come here to pray are often cured of their ailments. In the past, when the Tathāgata was a peacock king, he came to this place with his flock; driven by heat and thirst, they sought water but could not find any, so the peacock king pecked the cliff with his beak, causing a spring to gush forth. This has now become a pool, and those who drink from it or bathe in it are cured of their illnesses. Traces of the peacock still remain on the stone.

en_revised: One hundred and fifty li northwest of the statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one arrives at the mountain of Lamboura (藍勃盧山). On the mountain ridge is a dragon lake, over thirty li in circumference; its green waves are vast and expansive, and its clear waters are as bright as a mirror. In the past, when King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) attacked the Śākyas, four men resisted the army; they were expelled by their kinsmen and each fled in a different direction. One of these Śākyas, having left the capital, was exhausted from his travels and stopped midway. At that time, a wild goose flew before him; since it was tame and friendly, he mounted it. The goose flew and landed beside this lake. The Śākya, having traveled through the air far to a foreign land, was lost and did not know the way, so he took a nap in the shade of a tree. The young daughter of the dragon of the lake was wandering along the water's edge when she suddenly saw the Śākya; fearing her appearance was inappropriate, she transformed into human form and approached to stroke him. The Śākya was startled awake and asked, "I am a weary traveler, why do you show me such intimacy?" He then pressed her with great earnestness, forcing himself upon her in the wilderness. The woman said, "I have my parents' instructions, which I respect and do not violate. Although I am honored by your attention, I have not received their command." The Śākya asked, "The mountain valleys are dark and remote; where is your home?" She replied, "I am the dragon daughter of this lake. I respectfully heard that your noble clan was wandering in exile, and as I happened to be out for a stroll, I dared to offer comfort for your fatigue. Though we have come to intimacy, I have not yet heard my parents' will. Furthermore, due to accumulated karma, I have received this dragon body; humans and animals follow different paths, and such a thing is unheard of." The Śākya said, "If you grant me this one word, my long-held desire will be fulfilled." The dragon girl said, "I respectfully hear your command; I submit to whatever you decide." The Śākya then made a vow in his heart: "By whatever power of merit I possess, let this dragon girl's entire body be transformed into that of a human." Moved by the power of his merit, the dragon then changed her form; having attained a human body, she was deeply overjoyed. She thanked the Śākya, saying, "Due to my accumulated evil karma, I have been wandering in the lower realms. Fortunately, I have received your kind attention, and through the application of your merit, this wretched body held for vast kalpas has been transformed in an instant. I wish to repay this virtue, but even shattering my body would not be enough. I desire to accompany you, but I am constrained by the opinions of others. I wish to inform my parents, and then prepare the rites." The dragon girl returned to the pool and told her parents, "Today while out on an excursion, I suddenly met a member of the Śākya clan; moved by the power of his merit, I have been transformed into a human. My heart is set on a happy union, and I venture to state the facts." The Dragon King, pleased with the human realm and holding the holy clan in high regard, acceded to his daughter's request. He then emerged from the pool and thanked the Śākya, saying, "You have not shunned those of a different species, but have lowered your noble status to accommodate the lowly. I wish for you to grace my dwelling, where I dare to offer you service." The Śākya accepted the Dragon King's invitation and went to his residence. There, within the dragon palace, they prepared the rites for a personal wedding, and in the joy of their new union, they indulged in the utmost pleasure. However, the Śākya, seeing the dragon's form, felt constant fear and disgust, and wished to take his leave. The Dragon King stopped him, saying, "I hope you will not go far away, but reside in this neighborhood. I shall cause you to occupy territory, assume a great title, rule over subjects, and enjoy a long-lasting dynasty." The Śākya declined, saying, "This is not what I desire." The Dragon King placed a precious sword into a box and covered it with a fine white cotton cloth. He said to the Śākya, "I hope you will take this cloth and present it to the king. The king will surely receive this tribute from a man from afar in person, and at that moment, you can slay him. By then seizing his kingdom, would that not be excellent?" The Śākya accepted the dragon's instructions and went to make the offering. As the King of Udyāna (烏仗那) personally lifted the cloth, the Śākya seized his sleeve and stabbed him. The attendant ministers and guards clamored on the palace steps, but the Śākya brandished his sword and declared, "The sword I wield was bestowed upon me by the divine dragon to execute those who are slow to submit and to behead those who will not be subjects." All were awed by his divine martial prowess and pushed him to the throne. He then reformed the corrupt administration, honored the virtuous, and relieved the suffering. Having done this, he mobilized a great assembly and prepared a royal procession to go to the dragon palace to report his success and welcome the dragon girl back to the capital. The dragon girl’s past karma was not yet exhausted, and as her remaining retribution still persisted, whenever they were in private, nine dragon heads would emerge from her head. The Śākya, fearful and disgusted, did not know what plan to devise, but while she was sleeping, he used a sharp blade to cut them off. The dragon girl, startled from her sleep, said, "This is not to the benefit of our descendants. Not only is my life somewhat injured, but your offspring shall suffer from headaches." Therefore, the people of this royal clan often suffer from this affliction; although it is not continuous, it flares up from time to time. After the Śākya passed away, his son succeeded to the throne; this was King Uttarasena (嗢呾羅犀那王). After King Uttarasena succeeded to the throne, his mother lost her sight. After the Tathāgata had subdued the dragon Apalāla (阿波邏羅), he returned, descending through the air into the palace. King Uttarasena (嗢呾羅犀那王) had just gone out hunting, and the Tathāgata took the opportunity to briefly explain the essentials of the Dharma to his mother. Upon encountering the Holy One and hearing the Dharma, she immediately regained her sight. The Tathāgata asked, "Your son is of my clan; where is he now?" The mother replied, "He went out early this morning to hunt and is now about to return." The Tathāgata and the great assembly were about to depart. The King's mother said, "It is only by my good fortune that I gave birth into this holy clan; the Tathāgata has shown compassion and personally descended here. My son is just now returning, so I pray you stay and wait a moment." The World-Honored One said, "This person is of my clan. He can be awakened to faith by hearing the teachings; he does not require personal instruction to generate the resolve. I must go. When he returns, tell him: 'The Tathāgata is going from here to the śāla trees of the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城) to enter nirvana; he should take some of the relics for his own worship.'" The Tathāgata and the great assembly then departed, traversing the void. King Uttarasena was hunting when he saw from afar a brilliant light shining in the palace; suspecting a fire, he stopped his hunt and returned. He then saw that his mother had regained her sight, and rejoicing, he asked, "How long was I gone that such an auspicious response occurred, restoring my mother's vision as it was before?" His mother replied, "After you went out, the Tathāgata arrived here; upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, I regained my sight. The Tathāgata is going from here to the śāla trees of the city of Kuśinagara to enter nirvana, and he summons you to come quickly to share in the relics." When the king heard this, he wailed with grief and collapsed to the ground. After a long time, he regained consciousness and ordered his carriage to hasten to the site. By the time he arrived among the twin śāla trees, the Buddha had already entered nirvana. At that time, the various kings looked down upon him for being from a remote borderland; they prized the relics highly and did not wish to share them with him. Then, the assembly of devas and men restated the Buddha’s intention, and having heard this, the kings divided the relics equally, giving him his share first.

issues: The king, hearing this → 王或聞說: 或 = 惑, the king, deluded, heard her (Mizutani: 惑いをもって) | we have not yet been able to act upon it → 尚未可依: it should not yet be obeyed/trusted (Mizutani: なお信用はできません) | Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) monastery → 菩提樹伽藍, the Bodhi-tree monastery; Mizutani distinguishes it from the later Mahābodhi saṃghārāma (Beal: sangharama of the Bodhi tree) | The day after tomorrow → 吾於後日: on a later day, soon (Mizutani: 近く; Beal: To-morrow) | The powerful and wealthy families → 諸豪世俗 is ambiguous: 'the nobles and the common people' or 'the (implicated) nobles'; DM kept (Mizutani: 諸豪族; Beal: the common people)
en_revised: To the southeast of the city, on the northern side of the South Hill, there is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王) at the place where his son, Prince Kuṇāla (拘浪拏), had his eyes gouged out after being falsely accused by his stepmother. Blind people who pray here often have their sight restored. This prince was the son of the first queen; he was elegant in appearance and had long been renowned for his kindness and benevolence. After the first queen passed away, the stepmother, who was arrogant and lewd, gave free rein to her muddled stupidity and privately attempted to seduce the prince. The prince wept, took the blame upon himself, and withdrew to apologize for his perceived offense. Seeing her advances rejected, the stepmother’s fury intensified. Waiting for a moment when the king was at leisure, she said composedly, "Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅) is a strategic key to the kingdom; can it be entrusted to anyone other than a close royal scion? Now, the prince is known for his benevolence and filial piety, and because he is both a relative and a man of virtue, public opinion favors him." The king, deluded on hearing this, was pleased by the treacherous scheme; he immediately summoned the prince and admonished him, saying, "I have inherited the legacy of my ancestors to continue their rule, and I live in constant fear of losing it and thereby bringing shame upon the late kings. Takṣaśilā is the throat and belt of the kingdom, and I now appoint you to govern that country. The affairs of the state are heavy and complex, and the sentiments of the people are devious and mixed; do not act rashly or carelessly, lest you damage the foundation of our inheritance. Whenever there is a summons, verify it with my tooth-seal. The seal is in my mouth; how could there be any error?" Thereupon, the prince accepted the command and came to govern. As time passed, the stepmother’s anger grew; she forged a royal decree, sealed it with purple clay, and while the king was sleeping, she stole his teeth to make the impression, then dispatched a messenger to deliver the letter of condemnation. The assisting ministers knelt to read it, looking at one another in dismay. The prince asked, "Why are you so sorrowful?" They replied, "The Great King has issued a command, a written decree reprimanding the prince, ordering that your two eyes be gouged out and that you be exiled and abandoned in the mountain valleys, leaving you and your wife to live or die as fate decides. Although this command exists, it should not yet be obeyed. We should now request a confirmation, and you should present yourself bound to await your punishment." The prince said, "If a father grants death to his son, how can it be refused? The tooth-seal serves as the signet; truly, there can be no error." He ordered a Caṇḍāla to gouge out his eyes. Once his eyes were blinded, he begged for alms to sustain himself, wandering from place to place until he reached his father’s capital city. His wife said to him, "This is the royal city. Alas, the suffering of hunger and cold is truly bitter! Once a prince, now a beggar! I wish for us to make this known and have the previous charge re-examined." Thereupon, they devised a plan to enter the king’s inner stables. In the final watch of the night, weeping as he faced the clear breeze, he sang out in a long, mournful wail, accompanying himself on the konghou (harp). From his high pavilion, the king heard the elegant singing, the lyrics of which were deeply resentful and sorrowful; wondering at it, he asked, "The sound of the singing to the konghou seems to be that of my son; for what reason has he come here?" He immediately asked the inner stables, "Who is singing and wailing?" They then brought the blind man before the king. Seeing the prince, the king asked with suppressed grief, "Who has harmed your body and brought this calamity upon you? My beloved son has lost his sight, yet I remained unaware; how then can I investigate the affairs of all the common people? O Heaven, O Heaven! How has my virtue declined!" The prince wept piteously and replied apologetically, "It is truly because of my lack of filial piety that I have incurred the blame of Heaven. On a certain day of a certain month, I suddenly received your compassionate edict; having no way to voice my plea, I did not dare to evade my responsibility." The king, knowing in his heart that his second wife had acted improperly, did not investigate further but immediately imposed a severe punishment. At that time, there was a great Arhat named Ghoṣa (瞿沙) at the Bodhi-tree (菩提樹) monastery, who possessed unobstructed eloquence in the four analytical knowledges and was fully endowed with the three insights. The king brought his blind son and explained the situation to him, wishing only for his compassion to restore the boy's sight. After the Arhat accepted the king's request, he announced to the people of the country on that very day, "On a coming day I wish to preach the sublime truth. Let each person bring a vessel and come here to listen to the Dharma, so as to collect your tears." Thereupon, people from near and far flocked to the site, and men and women gathered like clouds. At that time, the Arhat preached on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; among all those who heard the Dharma, there was none who was not moved to deep sorrow, and they used the vessels they carried to collect their falling tears. When the preaching was finished, he collected all the tears and placed them in a golden basin, then made a vow, saying, "All that I have spoken is the ultimate truth of the Buddhas. If this truth is not genuine and my teaching contains errors, then so be it; but if it is not so, I wish to wash these blind eyes with the tears of the multitude, so that his sight may be restored and he may see as clearly as before." Having spoken these words, he used the tears to wash the eyes, and the eyes were immediately restored to sight. The king then rebuked his ministers and interrogated his officials; some were dismissed or banished, while others were demoted or put to death. The powerful and wealthy families were moved to the sandy desert to the northeast of the Snow Mountains (Himālaya).

issues: the mountain of Vyāsa (孤山) → 孤山 is 'a solitary hill', not a name; DM invents Vyāsa (Mizutani: 一つの孤山(離れ山); Beal: an isolated mountain)
en_revised: From here, traveling east for more than fifty li, one reaches a solitary hill (孤山). There is a monastery (saṃghārāma) there with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. Flowers and fruits are abundant, and the springs and ponds are as clear as mirrors. Beside it is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which marks the spot where the Tathāgata in the past converted an evil yakṣa, commanding him to cease eating meat.

issues: sought out both fame and reality → 幽求名實: probed deeply into names and realities (Mizutani: 名実(名目と実体)の理を求め) | I dare not forget my own unworthiness, and I wish to promote → 敢忘庸鄙，紹隆法教: I venture, forgetting my own mediocrity, to promote (Mizutani: 自らの凡庸なことも忘れて) | The king wished to hold the assembly in his own country, as he suffered from its heat and humidity → 王欲於本國，苦其暑濕: wished to hold it in his own country but was troubled by its heat and humidity (hence Rājagṛha) (Mizutani: その熱と湿気を心配して; Beal: suffered from the heat of 'this country', i.e. reverses) | 訖利多 rendered Kṛīta then Kṛta; inconsistent, left
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast, climbing mountains and traversing dangerous paths, crossing an iron bridge, and journeying more than one thousand li, one arrives at the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The country of Kaśmīra is over seven thousand li in circumference. Its four borders are backed by mountains; the mountains are extremely steep and precipitous. Although there are gateways and paths, they are narrow and constricted, and since ancient times, neighboring enemies have been unable to invade or conquer it. The capital city of the country faces a great river to the west; it measures twelve or thirteen li from south to north and four or five li from east to west. It is suitable for agriculture, produces many flowers and fruits, and yields dragon-breed horses, saffron (鬱金香), fire-pearls, and medicinal herbs. The climate is cold and harsh, with much snow and little wind. The people wear woolen garments and white cotton (㲲) clothing. The local customs are frivolous, and the people are mostly timid and cowardly. The country is protected by a dragon, and thus it dominates the neighboring regions. The people are beautiful in appearance, but their dispositions are deceitful. They are fond of learning and are well-informed, believing in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than five thousand monks. There are four stūpas (窣堵波), all built by King Aśoka (無憂王), each containing over a pint (升) of the Tathāgata’s relics. The *Country Records* (國志) state: "The land of this country was originally a dragon lake. In the past, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had subdued an evil spirit in the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) and wished to return to the Middle Kingdom, he rode through the air over this country and said to Ānanda: 'After my parinirvāṇa, there will be an arhat named Madhyāntika (末田底迦) who will establish a country here, settle the people, and propagate the Buddha-dharma.'" In the fiftieth year after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the arhat Madhyāntika (末田底迦), a disciple of Ānanda who had attained the six supernatural powers and possessed the eight liberations, heard the Buddha’s prediction and felt great joy in his heart. He then came to this place, sat in meditation within the woods of a great mountain range (大山嶺), and manifested great supernatural transformations. The dragon saw this and, deeply believing, asked what he desired. The arhat said, "I wish for you to grant me enough space within the lake to accommodate my knees." The dragon king then caused the water to recede and offered the space. The arhat used his supernatural power to expand his body, and the dragon king exerted his strength to shrink the water; the lake was emptied and the water exhausted, so the dragon turned and asked for the land back. The arhat left one pool for him to the northwest of this place, measuring over one hundred *li* in circumference; the rest of his kin were to dwell separately in smaller pools. The dragon king said, "The land of the lake has been entirely bestowed; I wish to provide offerings perpetually." Madhyāntika replied, "I shall soon enter parinirvāṇa without remainder; though I wish to accept your invitation, how would that be possible?" The dragon king requested again, "May five hundred arhats always receive my offerings until the Dharma comes to an end; after the Dharma has ended, I shall take back this country to serve as my dwelling lake." Madhyāntika granted his request. Once the arhat had obtained the land, he employed his great supernatural power to establish five hundred monasteries (伽藍). He purchased lowborn people from various foreign countries to serve as laborers and provide for the monastic community. After Madhyāntika entered parinirvāṇa, those lowborn people established their own rulers. The neighboring countries despised them for their lowly origin and would not associate with them, calling them Kṛīta (訖利多). At the present time, the spring water has largely overflowed. In the hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, King Aśoka (無憂王) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) ascended the throne to rule the world, his majesty extending to distant lands. He deeply believed in the Three Jewels and cherished all living beings. At that time, there were five hundred arhat monks and five hundred ordinary monks, all of whom the king revered and supported without distinction. Among the ordinary monks was one named Mahādeva (摩訶提婆), who was broad-minded and highly intelligent; he probed deeply into names and realities, and through profound contemplation, he composed treatises whose principles contradicted the sacred teachings. All who heard of them followed his divergent views. King Aśoka, unable to distinguish between the ordinary and the holy, sympathized with those he favored and sided with those he was close to; he summoned the community of monks to the Ganges River (殑伽河), intending to drown them in the deep current and execute them all. At that time, the arhats, being pressed by the threat to their lives, all exercised their supernatural powers, ascended into the void, and walked through the air, arriving in this country to dwell in the mountains and hide in the valleys. When King Aśoka heard of this, he was afraid; he came in person to apologize and requested them to return to their own country. Those arhats firmly refused to comply. King Aśoka built five hundred monasteries (僧伽藍) for the arhats and offered this entire country as a gift to the community of monks. King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) of the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國), in the four-hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, responded to the times and assumed the mandate to rule; his royal influence spread far and wide, and people of diverse customs submitted to his authority. In his leisure from state affairs, he frequently studied the Buddhist scriptures and invited one monk each day to enter the palace to explain the Dharma. However, the various schools held different and divergent views, and the king was deeply perplexed, unable to resolve his doubts. At that time, the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) said: "Since the Tathāgata passed away, the years have grown distant; the disciples have formed different schools, and teachers have held divergent views, each relying on what they have heard and seen, and all contradicting one another." When the king heard this, he was deeply moved and grieved; after sighing in lamentation for a long while, he said to the Venerable: "By my humble remaining merit, I have followed in the footsteps of my predecessors; though far removed from the Sage, I am still fortunate. venturing, despite my own mediocrity, I wish to promote and exalt the Dharma, explaining the Tripiṭaka in full according to the tenets of the various schools." The Venerable Pārśva said: "Your Majesty has planted roots of goodness in past lives and is richly endowed with blessings; that you should devote your mind to the Buddha-dharma is exactly what I desire." The king then issued a decree to near and far, summoning the sages and philosophers. Thereupon, they converged from the four directions, traveling ten thousand *li* like shooting stars; the brilliant and the virtuous all gathered, and the wise and the holy assembled in full. For seven days, he provided the four requisites as offerings. Wishing to hold a council on the Dharma, he feared it would be noisy and chaotic. The king then expressed his intentions to the monks, saying: "Those who have realized the holy fruit may stay; those who are still bound by defilements shall return." Even so, the number remained large. He issued another order: "Those who are 'without learning' (aśaikṣa) may stay; those who are 'still learning' (śaikṣa) shall return." It was still too numerous. He issued yet another order: "Those who possess the three insights (te-vidyā) and are equipped with the six supernatural powers (ṣaḍ-abhijñā) may stay; all others shall return." Yet it was still numerous. He issued a further order: "Those who have internally mastered the Tripiṭaka and externally attained proficiency in the five sciences (pañca-vidyā) may remain; all others shall return." Thereupon, four hundred and ninety-nine men were obtained. The king wished to hold the assembly in his own country, but was troubled by its heat and humidity, and so he also wished to go to the stone chamber where Mahākāśyapa (大迦葉波) had held the compilation at Rājagṛha (王舍城). The Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) and the others deliberated and said: "That is not possible. There are many non-Buddhists there, and their divergent views are tangled and confusing; one would be too busy responding to them to have any energy to compose a treatise. The hearts of the assembly are set on this country. This country is surrounded by solid mountains, guarded by Yakṣas (藥叉), the land is fertile, and its products are abundant; it is a place where sages and saints gather, and where spiritual immortals (靈僊) roam and dwell." The assembly agreed with this, and all said: "This is appropriate." At that time, the king and the Arhats came from there, established a monastery, compiled the Tripiṭaka, and wished to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘婆沙論). At that time, the Venerable Vasumitra (世友) was outside the door mending his robes. The Arhats said to Vasumitra: "Your fetters (kleśa) have not yet been eliminated, and your presence would disrupt our pure deliberations; you should depart to a distant place and not remain here." Vasumitra said: "You virtuous ones have no doubts regarding the Dharma and are spreading the teachings on behalf of the Buddha; you are now assembling the great meanings, intending to compose a definitive treatise. Although I am not clever, I have a rough understanding of the subtle words; I have also studied deeply the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka and the ultimate principles of the five sciences (pañca-vidyā), and have grasped their essence." The Arhats said: "One cannot speak like this. You should withdraw, quickly attain the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), and then join us; it will not be too late." Vasumitra said: "I regard the state of no-more-learning as no more than mucus or spittle; my ambition is to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and not to follow the Lesser Path." "I shall throw this ball of thread, and before it falls to the ground, I shall certainly realize the holy fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa)." At that time, the various Arhats rebuked him again, saying, "This is what is called a person of excessive pride (abhimāna). The fruit of no-more-learning is praised by all Buddhas; you should realize it quickly to resolve the doubts of the assembly." Thereupon, Vasumitra (世友) threw the ball of thread, but the devas in the air caught the ball and pleaded, "You are destined to realize the fruit of Buddhahood and will succeed Maitreya (慈氏) as the most honored one in the three realms (traidhātuka) and the one upon whom all beings of the four births (catur-yoni) depend; why do you wish to realize the lesser fruit here?" When the various Arhats saw this event, they apologized for their fault, acknowledged his virtue, and invited him to be the chairman (sthavira), and whenever there were doubts or discussions, they all took his decision as final. These five hundred sages first composed the *Upadeśa-śāstra* (鄔波第鑠論) of one hundred thousand stanzas to explain the *Sūtra-piṭaka* (素呾纜藏). Next, they composed the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘柰耶毘婆沙論) of one hundred thousand stanzas to explain the *Vinaya-piṭaka* (毘奈耶藏). Finally, they composed the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (阿毘達磨毘婆沙論) of one hundred thousand stanzas to explain the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (阿毘達磨藏). In total, there are three hundred thousand stanzas and nine million six hundred thousand words, providing a complete explanation of the Tripiṭaka to be preserved for all eternity; they exhaustively explore every branch and detail, investigating both the shallow and the deep, so that the great principles are clarified once more, the subtle words are again revealed, and through their wide circulation, later students may rely upon them. King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) then had the treatises incised on red copper plates, sealed them in stone cases, and erected a stūpa (窣堵波) to store them inside. He commanded the yakṣa (藥叉) spirits to guard the country, not allowing those of other schools to take these treatises out, intending that those who wished to study them should receive instruction within the country. When this work was completed, he returned with his army to his capital. He went out through the western gate of this country, knelt facing the east, and once again bestowed this entire country upon the community of monks. After King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) had died, the Kṛta (訖利多) tribe again proclaimed themselves kings, expelled the monks, and destroyed the Buddha-dharma. The King of Himatala (呬摩呾羅) in the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國) was a descendant of the Śākya (釋種) clan. Six hundred years after the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, he came to possess the territory and succeeded to the royal throne; he planted his heart in the Buddha-land and let his feelings flow into the ocean of the Dharma. Hearing that the Kṛta were destroying the Buddha-dharma, he gathered the brave and courageous men of his country, obtaining three thousand people, and disguised them as merchants. Carrying many precious goods and concealing weapons, they came and entered this country. The king of this country treated them with special courtesy. From among the merchants, he further selected five hundred men who were fierce and resourceful; each hid a sharp blade in his sleeve and, all carrying heavy treasures, they personally brought their offerings to present to him. At that moment, the King of Himatala removed his cap and took the throne. The Kṛta king was paralyzed with terror, whereupon he beheaded him and commanded the subordinates, saying: "I am the King of Himatala in the country of Tukhāra. I am angry at this base tribe for practicing tyrannical government, and therefore I have now executed the guilty one. As for all you common people, this is not your crime." However, he relocated the country’s ministers and officials to a foreign land. Having pacified this country, he summoned the monastic community, built monasteries, and settled the people as before. Furthermore, outside the western gate of this country, he knelt facing the east and offered the country to the monastic community. The Kṛta (訖利多) tribe had frequently caused the ruin of clans and the extinction of ancestral sacrifices on account of the monks, and for generations they had accumulated resentment and detested the Buddha-dharma. As time passed, they again proclaimed themselves kings. Therefore, at present, this country does not have much faith, and they pay special attention to the temples of the non-Buddhist devas.

issues: the great mountain (Pravaragiri) → 大山陽: the sunny (south) side of a great mountain; no name in the Chinese, DM's '(Pravaragiri)' is an addition (Mizutani: 大きな山の南側; he suggests Takht-i-Sulaimān)
en_revised: More than ten *li* southeast of the new city, north of the old city, and on the sunny side of the great mountain, there is a monastery with over three hundred monks. In its stupa is a Buddha’s tooth, about an inch and a half long and yellowish-white in color, which sometimes emits light on fast days. In the past, when the Kṛtīya (訖利多) race destroyed the Buddha’s Dharma, the monks dispersed, each living where they found it convenient. There was one śramaṇa who traveled through the various regions of India to observe and pay homage to the sacred sites, expressing his utmost sincerity. Later, hearing that his home country had been pacified, he set out on his return journey. He encountered a herd of elephants moving across the marshes, rushing about and roaring thunderously. Seeing this, the śramaṇa climbed a tree to avoid them. At that time, the elephants rushed together, vied with each other to suck up pond water to soak the roots of the tree, and then collectively pushed and dug at it until the tree finally toppled over. Having captured the śramaṇa, they carried him on their backs into a great forest, where a sick elephant lay suffering from a sore; it led the monk's hand to the afflicted spot, which had been pierced by a piece of withered bamboo. The śramaṇa then pulled out the bamboo, applied medicine, tore his robe, and wrapped the elephant's foot. Another large elephant brought a golden casket and gave it to the sick elephant, who, upon receiving it, passed it to the śramaṇa; when the śramaṇa opened the casket, he found it contained a Buddha’s tooth. The elephants surrounded him, and the monk had no way to leave. The next day at the time of the midday meal, they each brought exotic fruits to serve as his meal. After he had eaten, they carried the monk out of the forest, and only after traveling several hundred *li* did they set him down, whereupon each knelt in worship and departed. The śramaṇa reached the western border of the country and crossed a rapid river; when he reached midstream, the boat was on the verge of capsizing. Those sharing the boat said to one another, "The cause of this boat's impending disaster is this śramaṇa; he must possess a relic of the Tathāgata, and the dragons covet it." The boatman searched and indeed found a Buddha’s tooth. Then the śramaṇa held up the Buddha’s tooth and, looking down, said to the dragon, "I now entrust this to you, and shall return before long to take it back." He did not cross the river, but turned the boat back and departed; looking at the river, he sighed and said, "Because I lack the arts of subdual, I have been deceived by a dragon beast!" He went again to India to learn the methods for subduing dragons. After three years, he returned to his own country; when he reached the riverbank and set up an altar, the dragon then held up the casket of the Buddha’s tooth and presented it to the śramaṇa. The śramaṇa took it back and, at this saṃghārāma (伽藍), performed offerings.

issues: the great mountain (Pravaragiri) → 至大山: 'a great mountain'; no name in the Chinese (Mizutani: 大山; near Avantipur by distance)
en_revised: Traveling over thirty li southeast from the small monastery, one reaches a great mountain, where there is an old monastery. Its design was once magnificent, but it is now largely overgrown and in ruins, with only a small multi-storied pavilion remaining in one corner. There are over thirty monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings. Formerly, the śāstra-master Saṃghabhadra composed the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (順正理論) here. In the stūpas around the monastery, the relics of great arhats are preserved. Wild beasts and mountain apes gather flowers to offer them, never failing to do so throughout the year, as if following a command. There are many miraculous traces in these mountains, such as stone walls split horizontally or horse tracks left upon the peaks. All such phenomena, with their strange and unusual forms, are said to be the result of arhats and novices playing in groups, pointing and gesturing, or riding horses to and fro. Such traces are too numerous to describe in detail.

issues: *Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda-śāstra* (眾事分毘婆沙論) → a *vibhāṣā* on the Prakaraṇapāda, not the Prakaraṇapāda itself (Mizutani: Julien vibhāṣā-prakaraṇa-pāda-śāstra) | a śramaṇa in that country → 此國有一沙門: a śramaṇa of this country (Kaśmīra), not of East India (Mizutani: この迦湿弥羅国に一沙門がおり) | one-third of what I once did → 三分食一: I eat (only) one part in three; 'of what I once did' is DM's gloss, left
en_revised: More than ten li to the east of the Buddha-tooth monastery, among the cliffs of the northern mountains, there is a small monastery where the great master of shastras Skandhila (索建地羅) once composed the *Prakaraṇapāda-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (眾事分毘婆沙論). In the small monastery there is a stone stūpa over fifty feet high, which contains the bodily relics of an arhat. Previously, there was an arhat whose physical form was immense, and all that he ate was equal to that of an elephant. The people of the time ridiculed him, saying, "You only know how to eat your fill; how could you understand right from wrong?" When the arhat was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he told the people, "I shall soon attain the state of no-remainder; I wish to speak of the wonderful Dharma that I have personally realized." When the people heard this, they mocked one another, yet they all gathered together to observe his success or failure. Then the arhat said to the people, "I will now tell you the original cause and condition. Prior to this life, I received the retribution of an elephant's body in East India, where I lived in the king's inner stable. At that time, there was a śramaṇa of this country who traveled far to India to search for the scriptures and treatises of the holy teachings. The king took me and gave me to the śramaṇa to carry the Buddhist scriptures, and in this way, I arrived here. Not long after, I died. By virtue of the merit accumulated through carrying the scriptures, I was born as a human. Furthermore, blessed with remaining fortune, I donned the dyed robes early and diligently sought liberation, never resting, until I attained the six supernatural powers and severed the desires of the three realms. However, regarding what I eat, the residual habit remains; I always restrain myself, eating only one-third of what I once did." Although there was this account, people still did not believe it. He then ascended into the void, entered the fire-light samādhi (火光定), and smoke and flames issued from his body as he entered parinirvāṇa; his remaining bones fell to the ground, and a stūpa (窣堵波) was erected over them.

issues: Vikrītavana Monastery (商林伽藍) → CBETA 商林 'Merchants' Grove'; Vikrītavana rests on Julien's (and Beal's) emendation to 買林 (Mizutani notes both; Watters: merchants' grove)
en_revised: Traveling over two hundred li northwest from the royal city, one reaches the Merchants' Grove Monastery (商林伽藍; Julien emends to 買林, Vikrītavana), where the śāstra master Pūrṇa (布剌拏) composed the *Exposition of the Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (釋毘婆沙論).
